meta.theme: why languages change at a steady rate although no speaker intends it and prescriptive institutions have resisted it for centuries, answered by locating change at the point of transmission rather than of use, since each learner reconstructs a grammar from sentences that underdetermine it and may settle at the edges on a rule slightly unlike the one that produced them, a divergence that shows only in sentences nobody said, so resistance works exactly where it can be seen and change happens where it cannot

meta.reviewer_notes: The passage grants the objectors a real victory in its second paragraph, which is the sentence most readers skim, and every question in the set can be lost by concluding that resistance is futile. The attitude question is written against the corpus habit of keying the measured option: the author is warm towards the objectors and flatly certain they cannot reach the place change happens, and the detached candidate is the wrong answer rather than the right one.
meta.tone: curious, sympathetic to the objectors, quietly final

quality.adversarial_review: Q1's live rival is the option that change is inevitable and resistance always a waste of time, which the second paragraph refuses by crediting objectors with driving usages out of print inside a decade; the author's claim is about where resistance can reach, not about whether it works. Q2's rival is the option that campaigns have no effect at all, which is the conclusion a reader draws from the thesis rather than from the paragraph that states the opposite. Q3's rival is the option that two speakers who never disagree about a sentence must share a grammar, which the fourth paragraph denies in its first two sentences, since the divergence appears only in sentences nobody happened to say. Q4's rival is the detached option, because the corpus habit is to key the measured candidate; here the author has a definite stance, warm to the objectors and certain their effort cannot reach the place of change, and the paragraph on contempt and hope shows him judging rather than declining to. Q5's rival is the option about his own speech changing at the same rate, which converts a claim about a grammar improvised in childhood into a claim about continuing drift.

paragraphs.text: Every generation announces that the language is being ruined, and every generation is describing something real. Usages that were errors become acceptable, distinctions collapse, endings drop away. What makes the complaint interesting is not that it is wrong about the facts but that it sits so oddly beside two others. No speaker anywhere sets out to alter the language, since there is no advantage whatever in being misunderstood. And societies have maintained academies, style manuals, examiners and irritable schoolmasters for centuries, all pulling the other way. Yet the rate of change looks much the same in languages with such institutions as in languages without. Where does it come from, if nobody wants it and everybody is resisting it?

The usual answers do not fit the shape of the question. Laziness explains why an ending might be shortened and not why a distinction should be created. Youth explains who speaks differently and not why the difference survives after they are old. Contact with foreigners explains a great deal in some places and nothing at all in others. Each of the three accounts for particular changes; none accounts for the steadiness. And the assumption underneath all three, that resistance is simply too weak, is false. Resistance is not weak. A campaign against a single word or construction can drive it out of print inside a decade, and objectors have done exactly that, repeatedly. Wherever a speaker is choosing his words he can be argued with, shamed or instructed, and it works.

The place where it does not work is the place where a language is actually handed over. Nobody is given a grammar. Each learner builds one, in early childhood, out of the sentences that happen to be said near him, and those sentences do not determine the grammar uniquely. More than one rule will fit the evidence a child receives, particularly at the edges: constructions that are rare, patterns with few examples, the odd corner where a parent's own rule is applied perhaps twice a year. Where the evidence runs out the child settles on something, and what he settles on may differ slightly from the rule that produced the sentences he heard. He has not made an error. He has solved the problem he was given, and the problem did not have a single answer.

The difference is then invisible to everybody concerned, which is the crucial part. It shows up only in sentences nobody happened to say, so the child's speech is indistinguishable from his parents' across every case that arises, and no correction is ever prompted. Thirty years later he is himself the source of the evidence, and his own children build their grammars out of output that has already moved. Nothing has been decided, nobody has conceded anything, and no institution has been defeated, because nothing occurred that an institution could have attended to. Change enters a language at the one point where nobody is looking, and the resistance that works so well is stationed, necessarily, where everybody is.

What the objector meets, then, is the far end of something. A usage reaches the newspapers long after the settlement that produced it, which was made silently, in a nursery, by somebody who could not have said what rule he had adopted, and who could not say now. That is worth remembering on both sides of the quarrel. The objector's own grammar is equally unstatable and was equally improvised, which removes the grounds for looking down on him; and the usage he dislikes is not a lapse he has caught in time, which removes the grounds for hoping. The complaint is not foolish. It has simply arrived at the wrong address, and very late.

questions.target_mistake: converting a claim about where resistance can reach into a claim that resistance never achieves anything
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say before looking: change happens during transmission, where nothing is chosen and nothing can be corrected.
questions.stem: Which of the following best characterises the answer the passage gives to the question it opens with?

options.A: Change is driven by the young, whose speech the old resist for a while and in time adopt.
options.B: Change enters where transmission is imperfect and nobody is watching, so resistance is misaimed.
options.C: Change is the accumulated result of the small decisions speakers take in order to save effort.
options.D: Change is inevitable, so resistance to it has been a waste of everybody's effort.

explanation.expert_notice: The answer is built in two halves and both are stated flatly. The third paragraph locates change at the moment a learner reconstructs a grammar from sentences that do not determine it uniquely; the fourth says the resulting difference shows up only in sentences nobody said, so change enters where nobody is looking and resistance is stationed where everybody is.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option names the mechanism and the consequence for resistance in the passage's own terms. It has to include both, because the question the passage opens with is not merely where change comes from but how it survives determined opposition, and the answer is that the opposition is effective and misplaced. An option that makes resistance ineffective answers a question the passage has already declined to ask.
explanation.question_type_note: A characterisation question asks for the shape of an answer, not a fact from it. Where a passage opens with a puzzle, check that the candidate would actually dissolve the puzzle as stated.
explanation.reading_habit: When a passage poses a question with two awkward conditions attached, write both conditions down. The answer has to satisfy both, and most distractors satisfy one and quietly drop the other.

distractors.why_wrong: This is one of the three usual answers the second paragraph sets aside, and the objection to it is given there: youth explains who speaks differently and not why the difference survives after they are old.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the explanation almost everybody offers, and the passage's own account does place the decisive event in childhood, which makes the young look like the agents of change.

distractors.why_wrong: Effort-saving is the first of the discarded answers, and the paragraph says exactly what it fails to cover: it explains why an ending might be shortened and not why a distinction should be created. It accounts for particular changes rather than for the steadiness.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the most mechanical-sounding of the folk explanations and the one that feels scientific, and small accumulating decisions are the right general shape for an account of gradual change.

distractors.why_wrong: The second paragraph credits resistance with real victories, saying a campaign can drive a usage out of print inside a decade and that objectors have done it repeatedly. The passage's claim is about the layer resistance can reach, not about its strength.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the whole drift of the argument is that objectors cannot stop the process, and futility is the easiest conclusion to draw from an explanation of why they never win.

questions.target_mistake: answering from the passage's thesis rather than from the paragraph that credits campaigns with success
questions.stem: According to the passage, campaigns against a particular usage

options.A: make little difference, since change happens well below the level of choice
options.B: fail more often than not, because speakers resent being corrected by strangers
options.C: succeed chiefly where an institution such as an academy exists to enforce them
options.D: sometimes succeed, because conscious word choice is where resistance can act

explanation.expert_notice: The second paragraph makes the concession explicitly and then explains it. Resistance is not weak; a campaign can drive a word or construction out of print inside a decade; and wherever a speaker is choosing his words he can be argued with, shamed or instructed, and it works.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is those sentences compressed, with the reason attached. The detail is load-bearing rather than incidental, because the passage's answer depends on resistance being effective: if campaigns failed, the puzzle would have the ordinary solution that the objectors are simply too weak, and no account of transmission would be needed.
explanation.question_type_note: A detail question is decided by the sentence that states the fact, even where the passage's overall drift points the other way. Find the sentence before choosing.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author concedes that his opponents succeed at something, mark it. Concessions of that kind are usually load-bearing, and a set of questions will test whether you read them as concessions or as slips.

distractors.why_wrong: Resentment is never mentioned, and no rate of failure is given. The paragraph's claim about campaigns is positive: objectors have driven usages out of print repeatedly, and instruction works where choice is involved.
distractors.seductive_element: Correction does provoke resentment in ordinary experience, and readers supply a psychological reason where the passage has supplied a structural one.

distractors.why_wrong: The first paragraph says the rate of change looks much the same in languages with academies as in languages without, and the second attributes campaign successes to argument, shame and instruction rather than to any institution. The condition is that a speaker is choosing, not that a body exists.
distractors.seductive_element: Academies are named in the passage and are the obvious machinery for enforcing a usage, so a reader who remembers the word attaches it to the wrong claim.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph states the reverse in four words, saying resistance is not weak, and then gives the evidence. The passage's thesis is that change enters somewhere campaigns cannot reach, which is compatible with campaigns winning everything they can reach.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because it is the conclusion the rest of the passage seems to be driving at, and a reader who has grasped the thesis may answer from it instead of from the text.

questions.target_mistake: assuming that speakers who never disagree about any sentence must be using the same rules, which is exactly what the fourth paragraph denies
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that the implication will concern what a speaker knows without being able to say, or what agreement in practice fails to prove.
questions.stem: Which of the following is most strongly implied by the passage?

options.A: A language with a large written literature can be expected to change more slowly.
options.B: The grammar a child ends with is normally simpler than the one he learned from.
options.C: A speaker can follow a rule exactly without being able to state what the rule is.
options.D: Two speakers who never disagree about a sentence must be using the very same grammar.

explanation.expert_notice: Two places say it without saying it. The third paragraph has a child settling on a rule at the edges of the evidence, which he has not been taught and has not formulated; the fifth says the settlement was made by somebody who could not have said what rule he had adopted, and adds that the objector's own grammar is equally unstatable.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is the general form of those remarks. The whole mechanism requires that rules be followed without being available for statement, since a rule anybody could state would be a rule that could be taught, corrected and defended, and the passage's account of invisible divergence would collapse. The implication is a single step, and the passage takes half of it itself.
explanation.question_type_note: An implication question takes the author's claim one honest step. Prefer the option his mechanism could not do without over the one that merely sounds like his subject.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author says twice that somebody could not put something into words, treat it as a premise rather than as colour. Repeated remarks of that kind are usually holding up the argument.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage says what the child settles on may differ slightly from the rule that produced his evidence, and is careful to add that he has not made an error. Difference is not simplification, and no direction of travel is claimed anywhere.
distractors.seductive_element: Loss is what the first paragraph's complaints are about, with distinctions collapsing and endings dropping away, so a reader supplies simplification as the direction the whole process runs in.

distractors.why_wrong: Writing appears once, in the remark that a campaign can drive a usage out of print, and never as a brake on change. The passage's one comparison between languages goes the other way, saying the rate looks much the same whether or not the institutions exist.
distractors.seductive_element: A written record feels like a fixed point against which drift could be measured and resisted, and the passage does discuss institutions of exactly that kind.

distractors.why_wrong: The fourth paragraph denies this in its first two sentences. The divergence shows up only in sentences nobody happened to say, so two speakers can agree about every sentence that ever arises and still be running different rules, which is precisely why no correction is ever prompted.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because it states the reasonable principle that identical behaviour implies identical rules, and the passage's whole mechanism is built on the one case where that principle fails.

questions.target_mistake: reading the author as neutral because he is fair to both sides, when he takes a definite position about where the objectors' effort goes
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict a stance with two components: respect for the objectors, and certainty that their effort cannot reach the place change happens.
questions.stem: The author's attitude towards those who object to new usages is best described as

options.A: amused by the objectors, and pleased that their campaigns come to nothing
options.B: sympathetic to the objectors and sure their effort cannot reach the place of change
options.C: neutral between the objectors and their opponents, declining to judge the merits
options.D: alarmed by the speed of the change and impatient with those who deny that it happens

explanation.expert_notice: The attitude is built out of three sentences. Every generation is described as accurate about the facts; resistance is said to be strong and repeatedly successful; and the closing lines say the complaint is not foolish but has arrived at the wrong address, and very late.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option carries the warmth and the finality together, which is what those sentences require. The author defends the objectors twice, once against the charge of being wrong about the facts and once against contempt, and he is entirely definite that nothing they do can touch a settlement made silently in a nursery. Both halves are asserted, so an option that keeps only one of them misdescribes him.
explanation.question_type_note: An attitude question is answered from what the author says about the people, not from the drift of his conclusion. Fairness to both sides is not the same as having no view.
explanation.reading_habit: Collect the author's adjectives before you look at the options. A writer who calls a complaint real and not foolish, and its target unreachable, has told you his attitude twice and in two different registers.

distractors.why_wrong: Nothing here is pleased at the objectors' defeat. The final paragraph removes the grounds for looking down on them, on the ground that the objector's own grammar is equally unstatable and was equally improvised, which is a defence rather than a joke at his expense.
distractors.seductive_element: Writing about language complaints is usually written to mock them, and the author's calm about the inevitability of change reads as amusement to a reader expecting the genre.

distractors.why_wrong: He is even-handed about contempt and about hope, and he is not neutral about the question at issue: he says plainly that the complaint has arrived at the wrong address, which is a judgement about the objectors' case. Fair treatment of both parties is being mistaken for a refusal to decide.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the last paragraph really does address both sides in turn, and detached analysis is the safest-looking answer in any attitude question.

distractors.why_wrong: Neither half holds. No alarm is expressed anywhere, since the divergence is called slight, invisible and free of error, and the author's word for what the child does is that he has solved the problem he was given. Nor is anybody impatient with deniers: the first paragraph grants that every generation is describing something real.
distractors.seductive_element: The mechanism does describe grammars quietly separating across generations, which sounds ominous when it is summarised without the author's reassurances.

questions.target_mistake: treating a usage in the newspapers as a change still in progress, when the passage places the decisive event a generation earlier
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that the answer will put the objector at the end of a process rather than at its beginning.
questions.stem: It can be inferred that a speaker who objects to a new usage

options.A: would succeed more often if he could explain the older rule to the young
options.B: is meeting the visible end of a settlement that was made before he noticed anything
options.C: has failed to notice that his own speech is changing at the very same rate
options.D: is complaining about something no institution has ever attempted to prevent

explanation.expert_notice: The final paragraph puts the objector at the far end of something and dates the decisive moment: a usage reaches the newspapers long after the settlement that produced it, which was made silently, in a nursery. The fourth paragraph explains why nothing could have been noticed at the time, since the divergence appeared only in sentences nobody said.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that chronology stated as a fact about the objector's position. The inference matters because it explains the second half of the paragraph: the usage is not a lapse he has caught in time, which removes the grounds for hoping, and it could not have been caught by anybody, since at the moment it was settled there was nothing observable to catch.
explanation.question_type_note: An inference about a person's position in a process is answered by locating the process's decisive moment. Ask when the thing being objected to was actually decided.
explanation.reading_habit: When a passage explains why something is invisible while it happens, expect a question about the person who notices it afterwards. The answer is nearly always about how late he has arrived.

distractors.why_wrong: Explanation is a form of instruction, and instruction is said to work only where a speaker is choosing his words. The rule at issue was fixed in early childhood out of evidence that ran out, and nobody involved could state it, so there is nothing to explain and nobody to explain it to.
distractors.seductive_element: Teaching the rule is the objector's natural next move, and the passage does grant that argument and instruction succeed, which makes the recommendation look supported.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage makes the grammar a settlement reached in childhood, not a thing that goes on drifting through adult life, and its point about the objector is that his own grammar was improvised and is unstatable rather than that it is still moving. Nothing gives a rate for anything.
distractors.seductive_element: It reads like the clever reply an author of this kind usually makes to a complainer, and the passage does compare the objector's grammar to the one he dislikes.

distractors.why_wrong: The first paragraph lists academies, style manuals, examiners and schoolmasters as institutions that have been pulling the other way for centuries. The passage's claim is not that nobody tried but that nothing occurred at the decisive moment which any institution could have attended to.
distractors.seductive_element: The fourth paragraph does say no institution has been defeated, which a hurried reader converts into no institution having been involved.

vocabulary.passage_use: those sentences do not determine the grammar uniquely
vocabulary.meaning_here: in a way that leaves only one possible answer
worked out on the spot, without a plan or a model

vocabulary.passage_use: long after the settlement that produced it
vocabulary.meaning_here: the moment at which an undecided matter was fixed

vocabulary.passage_use: the resistance that works so well is stationed, necessarily, where everybody is
vocabulary.meaning_here: posted at a particular place, as a guard is

mentor.challenge: A question is asked in the first paragraph and answered in the third and fourth. Watch the second paragraph closely, because it grants the objectors a victory, and almost every wrong answer in this set comes from concluding that they never win anything.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: Languages change at much the same rate whether or not academies and schoolmasters resist, although no speaker intends any change, and the reason is that resistance operates only where words are consciously chosen while the language is actually handed over somewhere else, in early childhood, where each learner reconstructs a grammar from sentences that do not determine it uniquely and may settle at the thin edges on a rule slightly unlike the one that produced them, a divergence that appears only in sentences nobody said and therefore prompts no correction, so the objector always meets a settlement made a generation earlier and unstatable by anyone who made it.
mentor.main_idea: Nobody wants the language to change, institutions have resisted for centuries, and it changes anyway at a steady rate. The explanation is not that resistance is weak; campaigns against particular words work. It is that a language is rebuilt by every learner out of evidence that underdetermines it, so a child can settle on a slightly different rule without anybody noticing, because the difference shows only in sentences nobody happens to say. Change therefore happens where correction cannot reach.
mentor.simple_explanation:
Every generation says the language is being wrecked, and every generation is right about the facts. Mistakes become acceptable. Distinctions disappear. Endings fall off.

What is odd is how badly that fits with two other facts. Nobody is trying to change the language; there is no benefit in being misunderstood. And societies have kept academies, style guides, examiners and cross schoolteachers going for hundreds of years, all pulling the other way. Yet languages with all that machinery change at about the same speed as languages without it. So where does the change come from, if nobody wants it and everybody is pushing against it?

The usual answers do not fit. Laziness explains why an ending might get shorter, not why a new distinction appears. Youth explains who talks differently, not why the difference sticks once they are old. Contact with other languages explains a lot in some places and nothing in others. Each explains particular changes, none explains the steady rate.

And the assumption behind all three, that resistance is just too feeble, is simply false. Resistance is strong. A campaign against one word or one construction can wipe it out of print in ten years, and objectors have done that many times. Wherever a speaker is choosing his words, he can be argued with, embarrassed or taught, and it works.

The place it does not work is the place where a language actually gets passed on. Nobody hands you a grammar. Every child builds one, very young, out of whatever sentences happen to be spoken near him. And those sentences do not pin the grammar down. More than one rule fits the evidence, especially at the thin edges: rare constructions, patterns with only a couple of examples, the odd corner where a parent uses his own rule maybe twice a year. Where the evidence runs out, the child settles on something, and what he settles on may be slightly different from the rule that produced what he heard. He has not made a mistake. He solved the problem he was handed, and the problem did not have one answer.

Here is the crucial bit: nobody can see the difference. It only shows up in sentences that nobody ever happened to say, so the child sounds exactly like his parents in every case that actually comes up, and no one ever corrects him. Thirty years later he is the one producing the evidence, and his children build their grammars out of speech that has already shifted. Nothing was decided. Nobody gave in. No institution was beaten, because nothing happened that an institution could have been present at.

So change gets into a language at the one point where nobody is watching, and all that effective resistance is posted, of necessity, where everybody is.

Which means the person complaining is meeting the far end of something. A usage turns up in the newspapers long after the quiet settlement that produced it, made in a nursery by someone who could not have told you what rule he had adopted and still could not. That cuts both ways. The complainer's own grammar is just as unstatable and was just as improvised, so there is no ground for sneering at him. And the usage he dislikes is not a slip he has caught in time, so there is no ground for hope either. The complaint is not silly. It has just arrived at the wrong address, and very late.
mentor.why_difficult: The passage is organised around a concession that points the opposite way from its conclusion: resistance works, and works well, which readers find hard to hold while absorbing an explanation of why resistance never prevails. The second difficulty is that the mechanism turns on a negative fact, that the difference appears only in sentences nobody said, which has to be understood before either the invisibility or the implication about shared grammars makes sense. The third is the author's attitude, which is warm towards the very people whose project he says cannot succeed, so readers who expect either mockery or endorsement find neither.
mentor.author_intention: To stop the reader treating language change as a contest that somebody is losing, and to show him that the event he is arguing about happened years earlier, in a place where no argument was possible.

paragraph_journey.note: Languages change though nobody wants them to and institutions fight it, and the rate looks the same with or without the institutions.
Laziness, youth and foreign contact each explain some changes and not the steadiness. And resistance is not weak: campaigns really do win.
A grammar is rebuilt by each learner from sentences that do not pin it down, so at the thin edges he may settle on a slightly different rule.
The difference shows only in sentences nobody said, so no correction is prompted, and a generation later his output is the evidence.
He meets the far end of a settlement made silently years before. No grounds for contempt, and none for hope either.

mentor.tone_progression: It opens curious rather than combative, taking the complaint seriously as a description of facts, becomes technical and careful while the mechanism is laid out, and ends quiet and final, defending the objector from contempt in the same breath as it removes his hope.
key_transitions: 'And the assumption underneath all three, that resistance is simply too weak, is false.' (paragraph 2): the obvious answer is removed, which is what makes the puzzle hard.
'The place where it does not work is the place where a language is actually handed over.' (opening of paragraph 3): the answer arrives by relocating the question.
'The difference is then invisible to everybody concerned, which is the crucial part.' (paragraph 4): the mechanism's decisive property is named.
mentor.misunderstanding: The commonest wrong model is that the passage is another dismissal of pedants, in which complaints about usage are shown to be futile and faintly ridiculous. The second paragraph credits the complainers with winning repeatedly, and the last paragraph defends them from contempt. The second wrong model treats the account as a story about young speakers deciding to talk differently, which reverses the mechanism: nobody decides anything, and the divergence is invisible to the child as well as to his parents. The third concludes that speakers who understand each other perfectly must share a grammar, which is exactly what the invisibility of the difference denies.
mentor.traps_summary: This set offers futility in place of misdirection, the thesis in place of a paragraph that says the opposite, simplification in place of difference, detachment in place of a stance, and identical behaviour as proof of identical rules. Asking whether a claim is about the strength of resistance or about its location answers three of the five.
mentor.reading_lesson: When an author grants his opponents a real victory early on, treat the concession as part of the machinery rather than as politeness, because his thesis will be about the boundary of their success and every distractor will convert that boundary into a defeat. The companion habit is to watch for an author who is fair to both sides of a quarrel and still decides it: fairness of treatment is not neutrality of judgement, and the detached-sounding option in an attitude question is wrong whenever the author has said plainly which side has misunderstood its own case.
mentor.real_world: The same shape turns up wherever a practice is transmitted rather than taught: how a craft is learned by watching, how a family's manners pass on, how a profession's unwritten standards drift while its written code stands still. In each, the loud arguments happen at the level of stated rules, and the actual changes happen where somebody reconstructed a rule from too few examples and nobody could tell.
mentor.takeaway: A language changes not because anyone decided to change it but because every child has to guess it, and the guess is only visible a generation later.
mentor.reflection_question: Which of the rules you follow most exactly could you not actually state if somebody asked you to?
